questions.q: Why does carbon form a very large number of compounds? Explain the properties responsible.
answer: Carbon forms an enormous number of compounds, far more than any other element, because of two special properties.

answer.text: Carbon atoms have the unique ability to link with one another through strong covalent bonds to form long chains, branched chains and closed rings. This property, called catenation, allows countless carbon skeletons to be built up, each giving a different compound.

Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell and is tetravalent, so each carbon atom can bond with four other atoms, of carbon or of elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur. It can also form double and triple bonds, adding to the variety.
Because carbon is small, its bonds are strong and stable, so its compounds do not break down easily.

answer: Together these properties account for the vast family of carbon compounds.

questions.q: How do soaps clean dirty clothes, and why do detergents work better in hard water?

answer.text: A soap molecule has two ends: a long hydrocarbon tail that is hydrophobic, meaning it avoids water but mixes with oil and grease, and an ionic head that is hydrophilic and dissolves in water.

Most dirt is oily and does not dissolve in water. When soap is added, the hydrophobic tails attach to the grease while the hydrophilic heads face the water, forming tiny clusters called micelles that trap the dirt. When the cloth is rinsed and agitated, these micelles are washed away, taking the dirt with them.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts that react with soap to form an insoluble scum, wasting soap. Detergents do not form such scum, so they clean effectively even in hard water.

answer: This is why detergents are preferred where water is hard.
